title: Russia’s Hybrid War on Europe Escalates Yet Falters, IISS Says – Al Jazeera Report
body:
The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) concluded that Russia’s “hybrid war” against Europe – a blend of cyber‑attacks, disinformation, energy manipulation and covert sabotage – is intensifying, yet it has not succeeded in weakening Western political and material support for Ukraine. While Moscow’s unconventional tactics have caused measurable damage to critical infrastructure across the continent, the backlash has instead solidified NATO’s resolve and spurred a new wave of investment in resilience and security measures.

Since the start of the conflict in Ukraine, Russian operatives have stepped up campaigns that blur the line between state‑directed aggression and criminal activity. Recent weeks have seen a surge in ransomware strikes on hospitals in Poland, coordinated phishing attempts targeting energy firms in Germany, and a series of coordinated drone incursions that disrupted rail traffic in the Czech Republic. In addition, Moscow has leveraged its position as a major gas supplier to Europe, throttling deliveries and threatening price spikes as a lever to sow economic uncertainty. The IISS report notes that these actions have forced several European capitals to declare “national security emergencies” and to allocate unprecedented funds for cyber‑defence and critical‑infrastructure hardening.

Despite the growing frequency and sophistication of these attacks, the intended political payoff – eroding public appetite for continued aid to Kyiv – appears to be missing. Opinion polls across the EU show a steady or even rising level of support for military and humanitarian assistance to Ukraine, a trend that analysts attribute to the perception that Russian aggression is a direct threat to European stability. “Every time a Russian cyber‑attack hits a hospital or a power grid, the narrative shifts from ‘we’re being blackmailed’ to ‘we must stand together against a common enemy’,” said Dr. Elena Morozova, a senior fellow at the European Institute for Security Studies.

The failure of the hybrid campaign is also evident in the policy arena. The European Council has moved forward with a comprehensive “Strategic Resilience Package” that includes €50 billion earmarked for upgrading digital infrastructure, expanding redundancy in energy supplies, and establishing a joint European cyber‑response centre. Meanwhile, NATO has accelerated its “Enhanced Forward Presence” initiative, deploying additional cyber‑defence units to member states most exposed to Russian meddling. These steps signal a collective acknowledgment that the threat is not isolated to any single nation but is a systemic challenge requiring coordinated action.

Critics, however, caution that the escalation of defensive measures could trigger a further intensification of Russian tactics. Intelligence officials warn that Moscow may pivot to more covert operations, such as leveraging proxy networks to infiltrate supply chains or employing “false flag” cyber incidents to create confusion about the true source of attacks. The IISS warns that without sustained political will and continuous investment in resilience, the European Union could become vulnerable to a new wave of hybrid assaults that target emerging technologies like 5G and artificial intelligence.

Looking ahead, the trajectory of Russia’s hybrid warfare will likely hinge on the West’s capacity to adapt. If European governments can maintain public consensus on supporting Ukraine while simultaneously fortifying their own digital and physical infrastructure, Moscow’s strategy may remain ineffective. Conversely, any erosion of unity—whether through economic fatigue, political fragmentation, or successful disinformation campaigns—could open a window for Russia to achieve its broader objective of destabilising the European security architecture. For now, the evidence suggests that the hybrid war is evolving, but its core aim of deterring European solidarity with Kyiv is falling short.
